About this citation

Citations of the Apology in this archive are locators in Plato's dialogue, in which Socrates speaks. The archive files the passage under Socrates because he is the thinker being quoted, but Plato wrote the work, and the citation therefore names Plato and the page says who is speaking. The English wording is the translator's, so the locator identifies the passage while the quoted sentence belongs to a particular rendering of it.

Exact wording

English (as recorded here)
“The unexamined life is not worth living for a human being.”
Ancient Greek
“ὁ δὲ ἀνεξέταστος βίος οὐ βιωτὸς ἀνθρώπῳ.”

The Greek word order is “the unexamined life, not to be lived, for a human being.” Most English versions drop “for a human being,” which is where the claim is limited to a human life and not to life as such.

Forms in circulation that differ

  • “The unexamined life is not worth living.”
  • “An unexamined life is not worth living.”

Attribution notes

Socrates wrote nothing. This is Plato's rendering of Socrates' speech in the Apology, and the line falls in the penalty phase after the guilty verdict — Socrates is refusing a sentence of silence, not offering a maxim about self-help. Quoting it as a general exhortation to reflection drops the occasion it was spoken on.

About Socrates

Socrates (c. 470/469–399 BCE) was an Athenian citizen who wrote nothing and yet redirected Greek philosophy from cosmology toward ethics and the care of the soul.

Interpretation

Socrates says this while proposing a penalty after his conviction, so it is not a slogan about self-improvement but a claim about what a human life is for. The Greek verb behind "examined" belongs to the practice of testing a claim by questioning it. Socrates is arguing that a life run on untested opinions is not merely worse than a considered one, but not properly human, because the capacity to give an account of oneself is what distinguishes a person from an animal or a machine. The sentence is severe on purpose: he is about to tell the court he will not stop doing this even if acquitted on that condition.

Why it matters

The test is uncomfortable because it applies to opinions we hold for social reasons. A useful version: take one conviction you defend often, and ask what evidence would change it. If nothing could, you are not holding a view — you are being held by one.

Questions readers arrive with

What is the source of the quotation “The unexamined life is not worth living for…”?

“The unexamined life is not worth living for…” comes from Apology, 38a (c. 399–390 BCE), attributed to Socrates.

What does Socrates mean by life?

Life is both a biological fact and a practical project. Philosophers debate flourishing, suffering, mortality, and the standards by which a biography can be judged successful or wasted. This passage enters that discussion through life, wisdom.

Is the wording of this Socrates quotation commonly changed?

The wording recorded here is “The unexamined life is not worth living for a human being.” Forms in circulation that differ: The unexamined life is not worth living. / An unexamined life is not worth living. The Ancient Greek reads “ὁ δὲ ἀνεξέταστος βίος οὐ βιωτὸς ἀνθρώπῳ.”

Is this quotation attributed correctly?

Socrates wrote nothing. This is Plato's rendering of Socrates' speech in the Apology, and the line falls in the penalty phase after the guilty verdict — Socrates is refusing a sentence of silence, not offering a maxim about self-help. Quoting it as a general exhortation to reflection drops the occasion it was spoken on.
